description: We are 3rd year BSAI students looking to showcase our talent and skills that we have learned so far. Excited to participate in this hackathon.
summary:
Among the Stars is an educational website that works like a museum for the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors spin an interactive 3D globe of the Moon or Mars, click a glowing dot, and open an exhibit that explains why the machine was sent, how it worked, what scientists learned, and what became of it. Spacecraft that never landed get their own “Beyond” page, with distance and radio-signal-time notes. A    16-question quiz lets learners test themselves and get instant feedback.
The site answers the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten” by turning discarded equipment into memorable stories. It is written for learners aged about 10 to 14, in the friendly voice of a museum guide. It matters because these machines are part of humanity’s exploration history, and every fact is checked against NASA sources, with unverified details marked “Coming soon”. The site has no accounts or tracking and works offline.
details:
Among the Stars is an interactive web museum of the machines NASA left behind. Twelve exhibits ; four on the Moon, six on Mars, two still travelling beyond the planets , sit on a slowly turning 3D globe. Open one and you see what it did, where it is now, its mission timeline, its status in plain language, and the NASA page the facts came from.

How it works: A visitor starts on the homepage, opens the Moon & Mars globe, and clicks a pin or a name in the side list. The exhibit opens in place. They can filter by mission status, search by name, move on to "Beyond the Moon and Mars" for the spacecraft that never landed, and finish with a quiz of 16 questions — each one with an explanation and a link to its NASA source.Impact: The challenge asks for the story of NASA's abandoned equipment. That hardware is still out there, but there is no museum you can walk through. This one needs no ticket, no login and no download ,it opens in any browser and was written for curious learners around 10–14, in short sentences and a museum-guide voice.Tools: Hand-written HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no framework or build step, globe.gl for the WebGL globe, JSON data files as the single source of truth, and GitHub Pages for public hosting. Fonts are self-hosted (Orbitron and Exo 2, SIL Open Font License), so nothing depends on a CDN.

Creativity: The map itself is the exhibit, not a wall of text. Each machine keeps the place it actually stopped working, and the site treats "we don't know yet" as a real answer.

What we considered: Facts are checked against NASA's public mission pages and the NSSDCA catalogue; anything unconfirmed shows "Coming soon" instead of a guess. Status labels are precise and defined with a NASA source, and the same badge means the same thing on every page. Also: keyboard navigation and ARIA labels, layouts tested from 360 px phones to desktop, and image credits shown on every exhibit.
